key_terms.meaning: A computer built inside a larger product to do one dedicated job, often under real-time limits.
A requirement that a result must arrive within a fixed deadline, not just eventually.
A system whose output depends mainly on current inputs and events rather than a long stored program run.
Hardware and software designed together so each assumes the other's exact behaviour.
Program stored in non-volatile memory that controls the embedded hardware.
Running machine-learning inference locally on the device, close to the sensor.
Complexity, timing requirement, and form or connectivity are the three independent sorting axes.
A measurable property such as cost, power, size, speed, reliability or time-to-market used to judge a design.
A difficulty that must be solved while meeting metrics, such as power, real time, safety or cost.
Designing hardware and software together, moving functions across the boundary to meet metrics.
Software split into hardware abstraction, drivers, services or OS, and application layers.
A processor chip that needs external memory and peripherals to form a system.
A single chip with processor, memory and peripherals for control applications.
A processor optimised for repeated multiply-accumulate operations on digitised signals.
System on chip integrating processor, memory, peripherals and interfaces on one die.
Application-specific integrated circuit fixed for one function, with high one-time design cost and low unit cost at volume.
Field-programmable gate array whose digital logic is configured after manufacture.
Reduced instruction set computer with simple fixed-format instructions and many registers.
Memory organisation with separate instruction and data paths.
Non-volatile, electrically erasable and field-writable memory for code and data.

takeaways: An embedded system is a dedicated computer inside a product, shaped by real-time limits and constrained resources.
Sorting by complexity, timing and form or connectivity gives a useful classification without making one axis better than another.
Design metrics such as cost, power, size, speed, reliability and time-to-market compete, so each choice is a trade-off.
The hardware platform and layered software stack must be designed together, with a deliberate hardware-software boundary.
Processor choice follows the workload: microprocessor for general computing, microcontroller for control with integrated peripherals, DSP for signal arithmetic, SoC for integration.
RISC versus CISC and Harvard versus von Neumann are separate choices that affect instruction throughput, memory traffic and cost.
Memory selection is driven by volatility, field writability, speed and bits per rupee, and each type has a fixed role in the memory map.
Good answers connect definitions and block diagrams to a concrete small system: sensors, signal conditioning, processor, memory, communication and actuators.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine definitions, block diagrams, classification, design-metric trade-offs, processor and memory choices, and a small working example.

bank.q: Define an embedded system and explain six characteristics that distinguish it from a general-purpose computer.
outline: Definition: dedicated computer inside a larger product
Single function and little or no user interface
Constrained resources and low-power design
Real-time and reactive behaviour
Long life and high reliability
Tight hardware-software coupling with one clear example

bank.q: Classify embedded systems on the complexity, timing and form or connectivity axes, and give one example for each class.
outline: Three independent axes named correctly
Complexity: low, medium and high with examples
Timing: hard, firm and soft real-time with deadlines
Form or connectivity: standalone, networked, mobile and IoT
Examples tied to the correct class
Statement that an axis is not a quality ranking

bank.q: Explain the main design metrics and design challenges of an embedded system, and show three common trade-offs.
outline: Metrics: cost, power, size, speed, reliability, time-to-market
Challenges: power budget, real-time deadline, safety, testing, cost
Trade-off 1: faster processor versus power and cost
Trade-off 2: more memory versus unit cost and board size
Trade-off 3: higher reliability versus time-to-market
Use of measurable targets in a design review

bank.q: Draw and explain the hardware architecture and the layered software architecture of an embedded system.
outline: Hardware blocks: processor, memory, I/O, power, clock and reset
Sensors, signal conditioning, actuators and communication interfaces
Software layers: application, middleware or OS, drivers or HAL, hardware
Direction of calls and hardware access
Role of firmware and boot code
Where the hardware-software boundary can move

bank.q: Choose a processor for a battery-powered weather sensor that filters data locally and sends results over Bluetooth Low Energy. Justify the choice among microprocessor, microcontroller, DSP and SoC.
outline: Workload: sensing, local filtering, low-rate wireless transmission
Microcontroller with integrated ADC and wireless, or a small SoC
Why a microprocessor is wasteful: external memory and peripherals
Why a DSP alone is not enough for control and radio
Power, cost and board-size comparison
Final choice with a block diagram

bank.q: For a motor control loop, explain how timers, interrupts, ADC and PWM are used together. Include the interrupt service routine flow.
outline: Timer sets the control period
ADC samples current or speed
Interrupt service routine reads data, computes control and updates PWM
Short ISR and priority choice
PWM drives the motor driver
Safety limit and fault handling

bank.q: Compare RISC and CISC instruction sets, and Harvard and von Neumann memory organisations. Recommend one combination for a low-cost controller and justify it.
outline: RISC: simple fixed-format instructions, many registers, pipelining
CISC: complex variable-length instructions, fewer instructions per task
Harvard: separate instruction and data paths
von Neumann: shared path and the von Neumann bottleneck
Cost, speed and memory-traffic effects
Recommendation such as RISC with Harvard for a low-cost controller

bank.q: Select memory types for firmware, a calibration table, runtime stack and a frame buffer. Justify each choice using volatility, field writability, speed and cost.
outline: Firmware in flash or ROM
Calibration table in flash or EEPROM if field-updatable
Runtime stack in SRAM
Frame buffer in SRAM or SDRAM depending on size and bandwidth
Volatile versus non-volatile distinction
Memory-map placement and cost per bit

bank.q: Design a simple car parking sensor node. Draw its block diagram and explain signal conditioning, processor choice, memory use, output and timing.
outline: Ultrasonic or infrared sensor and signal conditioning
ADC or comparator input to a microcontroller
Processor and memory choice for small code and data
Buzzer or display output and distance calculation
Timer-based sampling and response time
Power supply and cost constraints

bank.q: Improving one design metric usually worsens another. Analyse this statement with examples from cost, power, performance and reliability.
outline: Metrics are linked through the design space
Faster processor raises power and cost
More memory raises cost and board area
Higher reliability raises testing and component cost
Low power may reduce peak performance
Conclusion: use quantified targets, not one blind maximum

bank.q: A system misses deadlines even though its CPU is fast. Analyse possible causes in memory, interrupt latency, bus contention and scheduling.
outline: Measure CPU utilisation and deadline misses
Long ISRs and interrupt latency
Memory wait states, cache misses and slow flash access
Bus contention with DMA or shared peripherals
RTOS priority inversion or poor task design
Fix by profiling, shortening ISRs, using DMA and adjusting priorities

bank.q: Evaluate ASIC, FPGA, SoC and microcontroller options for a product planned at 10,000 units and at 1,000,000 units. Consider NRE, power, performance and time-to-market.
outline: ASIC: high NRE, low unit cost, best at very high volume
FPGA: no mask NRE, higher unit cost and power, good for low volume
SoC: integration and performance with moderate NRE
Microcontroller: low NRE and fast development for control tasks
Volume threshold and time-to-market comparison
Final recommendation with numbers or ranges

bank.q: For an automotive driver assistance system, evaluate hardware-software co-design, safety, testing and debugging choices. Include sensors, processor, memory and actuators.
outline: Camera, radar or ultrasonic sensors and signal conditioning
Real-time processor or SoC with sufficient memory bandwidth
Hardware-software co-design for latency and safety
Redundancy, watchdog, fail-safe actuator behaviour
Testing, simulation, debugging and traceability
Trade-offs among cost, power, reliability and time-to-market

glossary.def: A device that converts an electrical control signal into physical action such as motion, heat or light.
Application-specific integrated circuit fixed for one function, with high one-time design cost and low unit cost at volume.
Complex instruction set computer with many complex, often variable-length instructions.
Direct memory access, a controller that moves data without the CPU handling every byte.
A processor optimised for repeated multiply-accumulate operations on digitised signals.
Running machine-learning inference locally on the device, close to the sensor.
Erasable programmable read-only memory erased by ultraviolet light and rewritten offline.
Program stored in non-volatile memory that controls the embedded hardware.
Non-volatile, electrically erasable and field-writable memory for code and data.
Field-programmable gate array whose digital logic is configured after manufacture.
A memory organisation with separate instruction and data memories and paths.
A high-impedance output state that disconnects a pin from the bus so another device can drive it.
An asynchronous signal that makes the processor jump to a service routine.
A single chip with processor, memory and peripherals for control applications.
A processor chip that needs external memory and peripherals to form a system.
A memory organisation with separate instruction and data caches or paths but one unified address space.
Non-recurring engineering cost, the one-time cost of designing and tooling a chip.
A resistor tying an input to supply voltage when nothing else drives it.
A resistor tying an input to ground when nothing else drives it.
A hardware event that puts the processor into a known start state.
Synchronous dynamic RAM clocked with the bus for high-density volatile storage.
A device that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
System on chip integrating processor, memory, peripherals and interfaces on one die.
Static RAM built from flip-flops, fast and volatile, used for caches and small data.
A counter peripheral that measures time or generates periodic events.
A memory organisation that stores instructions and data in one memory with shared address and data paths.
